e.etymology: An English surname, a spelling of Ash, for someone who lived by an ash tree. It also works as a short form of Asher and Ashley.

assoc.t: tennis champion Arthur Ashe and the US Open stadium
Ashe, a hero in Overwatch and League of Legends

e.etymology: Familiar as an old English pet form of Susan, also spelled Sukey, and from model and actress Suki Waterhouse. In Japanese suki means liking or fondness, though it is not a usual given name there.

assoc.t: Suki, the Kyoshi Warrior of Avatar: The Last Airbender

e.etymology: A name popular in Pakistani families, after Zunairah (Zinnirah), an early convert to Islam and companion of the Prophet Muhammad who was freed from slavery by Abu Bakr.
A modern coinage in the style of Lesly and Yesly, seen mostly in Spanish-speaking families. It may blend Jessica and Leslie; no meaning is established.
A spelling of Sidra, Arabic for the lote tree. In Islamic tradition the Sidrat al-Muntaha is the lote tree that marks the farthest boundary of heaven.
Latin for night, and the name of the Roman goddess of night, counterpart of the Greek Nyx. For boys it also reads as a pared-down spelling of Knox.
A girls' name used mainly in Pakistani families. Its source and meaning are not well documented.
An Albanian name, a variant of Eljon. In the US it also sits beside Elian and Elon, and it echoes Hebrew Elyon, Most High, a Biblical title for God.
A spelling of Corinne, the French form of Corinna, from Greek kore, maiden. Corinna was a lyric poet of ancient Greece.
From Latin Caelestinus, from caelestis, heavenly. Five popes took the name Celestine; in English it is now mostly a girls' name, by way of French Célestine.
The German and Scandinavian word for summer, and a surname from it. As an American girls' name it is mostly a respelling of Summer, which caught on in the 1970s.
A Scandinavian and German short form of Elisabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath. It is also well used in Latin America.
namesakes: Lisbeth Salander (heroine of The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo)

assoc.t: Lisbeth Salander, The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo

e.etymology: A surname from northern England and Scotland, from Old English baecestre, baker. The -ster ending first marked a woman who baked.
A respelling of Mackenzie, the Scottish clan surname from Gaelic MacCoinnich, son of Coinneach (Kenneth). It has been a girls' name in the US since the 1970s.
Anthony with the De- prefix that spread in African American naming from the 1970s on; often written De'Anthony. Anthony comes from the Roman family name Antonius, whose meaning is unknown.
From Arabic jalil, great or exalted. Al-Jalil, the Majestic, is one of the names of God in Islam.
A respelling of Bentley, an English place name and surname from Old English beonet, bent grass, and leah, clearing.

assoc.t: Bentley luxury cars, in the standard spelling

e.etymology: An old American given name of unclear source, probably an offshoot of Rena, a short form of names such as Irene, Serena and Renata. Renna is also an Italian surname.
From Arabic fa'iza, the feminine of fa'iz, a winner or one who succeeds.
A modern spelling in the family of Alina and Alanna, with the Aly- of Alyssa and the doubled n of Brianna. It has no separate meaning.
A respelling of Kylie, a name that began in Australia. Kylie is often linked to an Aboriginal Noongar word for a boomerang and is also treated as a feminine form of Kyle.
A spelling of Zuri, Swahili for beautiful. In Latin American families Zury is also a short form of Biblical names such as Zurisadai, built on Hebrew tsur, rock.
The name of the South American country, which was named for brazilwood, a tree with red dye wood that the Portuguese called pau-brasil, from brasa, ember.

assoc.t: Brazil, the largest country in South America

e.etymology: An English occupational surname, from Middle English schepherde, shepherd: one who tends sheep.

e.meaning: a wish or vow made in prayer
e.etymology: From the Hindi, Urdu and Punjabi word mannat, a wish or vow made in prayer, often at a shrine. It is especially common in Sikh families.
A modern American name, close to Asia and to Aziyah, in the pattern of Aaliyah and Amiyah. It has no established meaning.
From Arabic muntaha, the utmost or final limit. It is taken from Sidrat al-Muntaha in the Quran, the lote tree at the farthest boundary of heaven.
A modern American spelling of Malaya, in the pattern of Maliyah and Aaliyah. Malaya is also the Tagalog word for free and an old name for the Malay Peninsula.
A spelling of Aila or Ayla. Aila is a Finnish name of Sami origin; Ayla is Turkish, from ay, moon, and also a spelling of Hebrew Elah, terebinth tree.
A K-spelling of Camilo, the Spanish form of the Roman family name Camillus, probably Etruscan and of unknown meaning. In Latin a camillus was a boy who served at religious rites.
The English word coast, the land along the sea, respelled with a K in the manner of Kash and Kolt.

e.note: Melona is also a Korean brand of melon ice cream bars sold in many US grocery stores.
